results.title: Contrast vs. Non-Contrast CT Scans | MXR Imaging
results.content: ## **What are the differences between CT scans with contrast versus without contrast?**. CT scanners use X-rays to capture diagnostic images of the internal structures and organs of a patient. CT scans are used for many different reasons, including to inspect a patient's bones for fractures as well to examine the brain and abdomen. When preparing a patient for a CT scan, the doctor may choose to order a CT scan with or without contrast. The use of contrast in a CT scan depends on what part of the body is being scanned and what the doctor is looking for in particular. Contrast is a dye that is administered to the patient before a CT scan is performed. It's worth noting that when used for a contrast, it will not permanently dye any of a patient's internal structures or organs. * **Gadolinium-based contrast** - Gadolinium is similar to iodine and is a heavy metal that's capable of attenuating X-rays; however, it tends to have a lower visibility on CT scans than iodine.

results.title: Tricky terms explained: Non-contrast vs contrast CT scan - SCP Radiology
results.content: *Your doctor might write a referral for a CT scan, either with or without contrast. What is the difference between a non-contrast and a contrast CT scan, and when is contrast necessary?*. A CT scan, or a computed tomography scan, is a medical imaging procedure that uses X-rays and computer technology to create detailed cross-sectional images of the body. ### A contrast-enhanced CT scan. This is when a contrast agent (typically iodine-based) is injected into a patient’s bloodstream, usually through an IV line, during the scanning procedure. ### A non-contrast CT scan. Unlike contrast-enhanced CT scans, which involve the injection of a contrast into the bloodstream to highlight certain structures or abnormalities, a non-contrast CT scan is performed without the use of any intravenous contrast. Non-contrast CT scans are also useful in situations where the use of contrast agents may be contraindicated, such as in patients with kidney problems or allergies to contrast.

results.content: Published Time: 2019-07-10T12:17:10+00:00 What Is The Difference Between Contrast and Non-contrast CT Scans by Dr Adil Maqbool What Is The Difference Between Contrast and Non-contrast CT Scans 7 min read July 10, 2019 A CT scan also referred to as computed tomography scan, is a medical technique of producing cross-sectional images of particular areas of the scanned part of the body with the help of computer-processed combinations of many x-rays which are recorded from different angles. Among these forms, two widely known ones are contrast computed tomography scan and non-contrast computed tomography scan. A non-contrast CT scan is a kind of computed tomography scan which is carried out without using a special dye meant to make organs more prominent. CT scans can be done with or without contrast, determined by the medical circumstances of each different case. A combination of x-rays technology and computer imaging is needed to perform computed tomography scans [CT Scans]. Both contrast and non-contrast CT scans are regarded as safe procedures having minimal risk and thousands of people worldwide go through these processes every year. “Dyes” act as contrast agents during a CT scan process. Oral contrast is usually for highlighting the gastrointestinal organs in the pelvis and abdomen. The patient which is to go through oral contrast is directed to fast for a couple of hours before being administered this contrast. The organs that have swallowed the contrast look as a highlighted white section on CT image. The contrast agent (usually an iodine compound) is clear, with a water-like consistency. * The most notable side effect of the said contrast agent is a warm or “flushed” sensation during the process of injection of iodine. * Doctors usually use an enema, also known as a clyster, to administer rectal CT contrast. After the completion of CT, the contrast is eliminated and the patient may visit the bathroom. * Similar preparations are also needed for rectal contrast as were in oral contrast; patient here too has to fast for many hours before being going through the test. While guidelines such as the Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease (2023 update) do not directly address this issue, others explicitly recommend non-contrast chest CT, especially in the assessment for lung volume reduction therapy.4–600117-5/fulltext#). Multi-energy techniques like dual-energy CT or photon-counting CT could close this gap by calculating virtual non-contrast images (VNC) from contrast-enhanced scans without needing a separate unenhanced scan. So far, only a few studies have compared true non-contrast (TNC) and VNC images in quantitative chest CT. Mean ± standard deviation of quantitative CT measurements for virtual non-contrast (VNC) and true non-contrast (TNC) scans are reported, separated by volumes of interest. Bland–Altman analysis (mean difference with 95% confidence intervals and limits of agreement) of virtual non-contrast minus true non-contrast measurements (VNC – TNC) is reported. Lower MLD values in the VNC images were also observed for the lung center compared with the lung periphery (mean difference, -0.98 HU [-5.54, 3.59] vs. We found no evidence of a difference for the mean differences between VNC and TNC scans for all volumes of interest when dividing the patient collective by the median BMI or median LAV (as a measurement of pulmonary emphysema) with Bonferroni-corrected _P_ values >.05 for all comparisons. Consequently, we present the first study to compare intrapulmonary regional differences in quantitative measurements of virtual and true non-contrast chest CT scans (VNC vs. They report significant differences in LAV regarding the whole cohort but not when only considering patients with a normal body mass index, concluding that VNC images are an acceptable substitute for non-enhanced scans in individuals with “a normal body composition”.700117-5/fulltext#). Jungblut _et al._ used a photon-counting detector CT to generate VNC images and compared these with unenhanced scans in a cohort of 65 patients, reporting similar results for emphysema quantification.800117-5/fulltext#). In conclusion, our study demonstrated a high correlation and agreement between virtual and true non-contrast scans for parameters typically assessed in emphysema quantification (MLD, LAV, 15th percentile), potentially obviating additional non-contrast scans.
